source_batch.unit_label: Module B unit 4 (courseware unit 13), gap closure: the four Labour Codes in force from 21 November 2025

facts.statement: The Government made four Labour Codes effective from 21 November 2025: the Code on Wages, 2019, the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, the Code on Social Security, 2020 and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, rationalising 29 existing labour laws. The Code on Wages was notified on 8 August 2019 and the other three on 29 September 2020. During the transition, the relevant provisions of the existing labour Acts and their rules, regulations, notifications, standards and schemes continue to remain in force while rules under the Codes are framed. The Codes introduce the idea of a single registration, single licence and single return to reduce the compliance burden.

The Code on Wages, 2019 rationalises four laws: the Payment of Wages Act, 1936, the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 and the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976. Main provisions: a statutory right to minimum wages for all employees in organised and unorganised sectors (the earlier Act covered scheduled employments, about 30 per cent of workers); a statutory floor wage set by the Government on minimum living standards, below which no State may fix minimum wages; minimum wages fixed with regard to skill levels, geographical area and job conditions; employers shall not discriminate on the basis of gender, including transgender identity, in recruitment, wages and conditions of employment for similar work; provisions on timely payment and unauthorised deductions apply to all employees irrespective of wage limit (earlier only employees earning up to Rs 24,000 a month); overtime wages of at least twice the normal rate for work beyond regular hours; replacement of the Inspector by an Inspector-cum-Facilitator; compounding of first-time non-imprisonable offences (repeat offences within five years cannot be compounded); and replacement of imprisonment for some first-time offences by fines.

The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 amalgamates the Trade Unions Act, 1926, the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 and the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. Main provisions: fixed term employment with full parity in wages and benefits and gratuity after one year; a re-skilling fund for retrenched employees financed by 15 days' wages for every worker retrenched, in addition to retrenchment compensation, credited to the worker's account within 45 days; a union with 51 per cent membership is recognised as the Negotiating Union, otherwise a Negotiating Council is formed from unions with at least 20 per cent membership; the definition of worker covers sales promotion staff, journalists and supervisory employees earning up to Rs 18,000 a month; the approval threshold for lay-off, retrenchment and closure rises from 100 to 300 workers (States may raise it further) and the standing orders threshold from 100 to 300 employees; proportional representation of women in grievance committees; work from home in service sectors by mutual consent; two-member Industrial Tribunals; direct approach to the tribunal after failed conciliation within 90 days; a mandatory 14-day notice for strikes and lockouts in all establishments; and a definition of strike that includes mass casual leave.

The Code on Social Security, 2020 incorporates nine Acts: the Employee's Compensation Act, 1923, the Employees' State Insurance Act, 1948, the Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952, the Employment Exchanges (Compulsory Notification of Vacancies) Act, 1959, the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961, the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, the Cine-Workers Welfare Fund Act, 1981, the Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Cess Act, 1996 and the Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act, 2008. Main provisions: social security for all workers including gig and platform workers (new definitions of aggregator, gig worker and platform worker, with aggregators contributing 1 to 2 per cent of annual turnover, capped at 5 per cent of the amount paid or payable to gig and platform workers); ESIC applies pan-India without the notified-areas criterion, with voluntary opt-in for establishments with fewer than 10 employees; a uniform definition of wages in which 50 per cent of total remuneration (or a notified percentage) is added back to compute wages; gratuity for fixed-term employees after one year instead of five; dependants extended to maternal grandparents and, for female employees, dependent parents-in-law; accidents while commuting between home and workplace treated as employment-related; and a social security fund for unorganised, gig and platform workers.

The Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 amalgamates the relevant provisions of 13 Central Acts including the Factories Act, 1948, the Plantations Labour Act, 1951, the Mines Act, 1952, the Motor Transport Workers Act, 1961, the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 and the Building and Other Construction Workers Act, 1996. Main provisions: electronic registration for establishments with 10 or more employees, one registration in place of six; extension to any establishment, even with one employee, engaged in hazardous or life-threatening occupations; women may work in all types of establishments and during night hours (before 6 AM and beyond 7 PM) with consent and safety measures; appointment letters specifying job details, wages and social security; free annual health check-ups; factory thresholds raised from 10 to 20 workers (with power) and from 20 to 40 workers (without power); contract labour applicability raised from 20 to 50 workers, with an all-India licence valid for 5 years; safety committees for establishments with 500 or more workers; and compounding of fine-only offences by paying 50 per cent of the maximum fine (75 per cent where imprisonment or fine or both applies).

payload.title: Four small calculations under the Codes
payload.core_explanation_md: An employee's normal rate is Rs 150 per hour. (a) He works 4 hours of overtime: find the minimum overtime pay. (b) A worker is retrenched whose wage is Rs 900 per day: find the amount credited to the re-skilling fund. (c) An aggregator has annual turnover of Rs 500 crore and pays Rs 150 crore to gig workers, and is liable at 2 per cent of turnover subject to the 5 per cent cap on payments to gig workers: find its contribution. (d) A fine-only offence carries a maximum fine of Rs 1,00,000: find the compounding amount.

worked_steps.description: Overtime is paid at least twice the normal rate.
Cap at 5 per cent of payments to gig workers.
The contribution is the lower of the two.
Fine-only offences are compounded at 50 per cent of the maximum fine.

unresolved: Facts come from two government press documents (a PIB release and a PIB backgrounder, both of 21 November 2025). They summarise the four Labour Codes; the statutes, the rules under them and any later amendment or deferral were not read. Thresholds and rates are as the backgrounder states them.

The courseware's statements on the Equal Remuneration Act 1976, Factories Act 1948, Hindu Succession Act 1956, Indian Penal Code section 354 and the PoSH Act 2013 (Module B unit 3) are NOT taught: this batch only verifies that the Code on Wages absorbs the Equal Remuneration Act and the OSH Code absorbs the Factories Act. The gaps for the Hindu Succession Act, the replacement of the Indian Penal Code and the PoSH Act statement remain open.

The courseware's account of Bipartite Settlements and the productivity linked incentive under the IXth settlement is not touched. The Payment of Bonus Act 1965 is among the laws the Code on Wages absorbs; its bonus provisions were not read.
Reviewer for this batch is the authoring agent; no independent or human review.
